title: Another NBA ownership change: Control of Timberwolves changes hands at $4.5 billion price tag - CBS Sports
description: Stad will become the controlling owner after buying the majority of co-owner Marc Lore's stake
body:
Stad will become the controlling owner after buying the majority of co-owner Marc Lore's stake
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:31 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Minnesota Timberwolves and Minnesota Lynx have been sold for the second time in as many years, as Marc Lore has agreed to sell his majority stake in the franchises to tech investor Marc Stad, per multiple reports. Stad, who was already a limited partner in the franchises, is purchasing Lore's majority stake at a $4.5 billion valuation. Lore purchased the Timberwolves along with Alex Rodriguez from Glen Taylor for $1.5 billion in a deal that was first initiated in 2021 but took years to fully execute and included a protracted legal battle that ended last summer with the team officially transitioning to Lore and Rodriguez's ownership. Now, 14 months after Lore finally became the majority owner, he is selling his stake to focus on taking Wonder, his food delivery company, public. Rodriguez will reportedly stay on and is investing further by purchasing more shares to increase his stake in the team. Stad, per The Athletic, is committed to keeping the Wolves and Lynx in Minnesota and will continue a push to build a new arena. The latest Timberwolves sale creates a rather bizarre trend of NBA teams selling -- and then selling again. Lore selling just a year into his official tenure as the franchise's owner (with a $3 billion increase in valuation) comes a week after Mark Walter did the same with the record-setting sale of the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion. 
Walter's situation was unique, given his ongoing legal troubles as he faces a federal investigation over his finances. Lore selling raises eyebrows for a different reason. NBA franchises have seen their valuations skyrocket in recent years, particularly with the league's new $77 billion national TV deal in place, and many longtime owners have opted to cash in on the increases by selling. Ten teams -- the Lakers, Celtics, Trail Blazers, Timberwolves, Mavericks, Rockets, Suns, Hornets, Jazz and Nets -- have sold in the past decade, with the Lakers and Wolves now selling twice in that span. 
        
            
                Jeanie Buss disputes her family's sale of Lakers stake: What to know about dramatic off-court fight
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Sports franchises were once seen as vanity projects for the ultra-wealthy, but now are viewed as key business holdings and owners are treating them as such. That has led to more buying and selling over the last decade-plus, with the valuation of the Timberwolves and Lynx tripling in the five years since Lore first began purchasing the team in 2021. It presented an opportunity to cash out at a significant profit. 
The concern for fans, of course, is that teams being treated as investments to be flipped more often can mean a lack of stability -- and the ever-present concern for small-market clubs that new ownership groups without ties to the area could push to move the franchise. Portland is currently in a contentious battle with new owner Tom Dundon over funding for arena renovations. Dundon has not been shy about his willingness to move the franchise if his demands aren't met. That doesn't appear to be a concern in Minnesota in the immediate future, but plans to build a new arena can always bring tension over the allocation of public funds. Perhaps the Lakers and Timberwolves will end up as anomalies, but if more teams start being bought and flipped, it will raise concerns for the NBA about ownership stability and about building the kind of connection and trust needed with fans.

title: Sergio Garcia incident at the Masters may caused LIV Golf to lose funding, per report - CBS Sports
description: Garcia smashing his club at the Masters might have been a bigger deal than anyone ever imagined
body:
Garcia smashing his club at the Masters might have been a bigger deal than anyone ever imagined
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:38 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        LIV Golf is currently playing its final event of the 2026 season in Indianapolis. Once Sunday's final round ends, the future of the tour is up in the air after losing its funding from the Saudi Arabia PIF earlier this year.  The shocking news that the PIF was pulling the plug on its LIV Golf investment came out mere days after the 2026 Masters as LIV Golf was preparing for its event in Mexico City. Apparently, that timing wasn't a mere coincidence, but the events of the week prior in Augusta, Georgia, may have accelerated the PIF's decision to pull the plug. According to the Financial Times, Sergio Garcia's meltdown on the 2nd tee on Sunday at the Masters embarrassed Yasir al-Rumayyan -- the governor of the PIF who had been at the helm of LIV Golf since its inception -- and played a role in his decision to pull LIV's funding. Here's the report:
In April, as LIV golfers floundered at the Masters, golf's most prestigious tournament, Spanish star Sergio Garcia damaged the Augusta National course during a fit of rage in the final round.People familiar with the matter say Rumayyan's embarrassment at the sequence of events helped lead to his decision to pull the plug on PIF's financing of the rival tour, as the fund focuses more on its huge domestic commitments in the kingdom.
Garcia received a warning for violating the major championships' new code of conduct and issued an apology afterwards. Rumayyan's desire to become a member at Augusta National has been well-reported, and Garcia's tantrum did not reflect well on the LIV Golf boss. As Joel Beall of Golf Digest noted in wake of the FT report, the discussions internally about the PIF pulling its funding from LIV Golf had begun prior to Garcia smashing his club, so it wasn't the cause of the decision. That said, given how hastily things moved from that point with the PIF backing out within days of the final round of the Masters, it does seem fair to wonder if the incident accelerated the timeline. 
LIV declined to comment when asked by the Financial Times about the situation and we will likely never know for certain how significant a role it played, but it's a wild to imagine that Garcia smashing his club on Sunday morning at the Masters might've shifted billions of dollars in the golf industry and accelerated LIV Golf's demise.

title: Arsenal vs. Coventry City live stream: Where to watch Premier League online - CBS Sports
description: Arsenal enter the season as defending champions and will kicking things off against newly promoted side Coventry
body:
Arsenal enter the season as defending champions and will kicking things off against newly promoted side Coventry City, which marks the first game of the new campaign
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    2:15 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
No two Premier League seasons are ever exactly alike but as a new one begins this weekend, there is an unusually unpredictable – and exciting – feeling to this one.Most of the league's 20 teams enter the new campaign in some form of transition, be it through new managers, squad turnover or the task of successfully making the jump from the Championship to the top flight. Naturally, a few constants still hold true. Reigning champions Arsenal remain mostly unchanged from last season's triumphs and, after several years of continuity, look to repeat as title winners. The promoted trio of Coventry City, Ipswich Town and Hull City will also have their work cut out for them, the odds of staying up not exactly in their favor. Everything else, though, is up in the air.The opening round of games will offer a first real glimpse at the many, many teams who return to play with new plans, while the early weeks of the season will help fill in the gaps as onlookers begin to learn each team's new patterns. That said, several key matchups will be particularly revealing. Manchester City, now without ex-coach Pep Guardiola and midfielder Rodri, will take on a Bournemouth side under new management of their own but eager to build upon last season's results that saw them qualify for European competition for the first time. Chelsea's clash with Fulham, meanwhile, marks a meeting between last season's Real Madrid managers – Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa, each with a different point to prove.The new season opens on Friday with a battle between England's most recent champions, Arsenal and Championship winners Coventry City.Here's what you need to know as a new season begins.Premier League opening weekend scheduleAll times U.S./EsternFriday, Aug. 21Arsenal vs. Coventry City, 3 p.m. (USA Network)Saturday, Aug. 22Hull City vs. Manchester United, 7:30 a.m. (USA Network)Everton vs. Crystal Palace, 10 a.m. (USA Network)Ipswich Town vs. Sunderland, 10 a.m. (Peacock)Nottingham Forest vs. Leeds United, 10 a.m. (Peacock)Brentford vs. Tottenham Hotspur, 12:30 p.m. (Peacock)Sunday, Aug. 23Manchester City vs. Bournemouth, 9 a.m. (USA Network)Brighton and Hove Albion vs. Aston Villa, 9 a.m. (Peacock)Newcastle United vs. Liverpool, 11:30 a.m. (USA Network)Monday, Aug. 24Fulham vs. Chelsea, 3 p.m. (USA Network)New managers everywhere you lookNine teams enter the new season with new managers, while Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur begin the new campaign with coaches who are in their first full seasons in charge. It leaves a lot of entertaining uncertainty in every section of the table, but most intriguing at the top end. The Gunners would have gone in as the favorites to repeat as champions regardless of what their opponents got up to over the summer but at this point of the season, it's hard to know who – if any – will mount a reasonable challenge. The questions facing each of them are meaty, too. Will Enzo Maresca be able to transition smoothly into his new role at City after Pep Guardiola's storied decade in charge? Can Xabi Alonso steer Chelsea in the right direction after years of ups and downs under the new owners – and put the chaos of Real Madrid behind him? Will Andoni Iraola find a way to get Liverpool's high-profile attacking unit going after last summer's spending spree? Are Manchester United normal now?Can the promoted teams stay up?Even amidst a sea of change in the Premier League, some things always stay the same. That includes the grueling fight for survival for the teams who earned promotion from the Championship, none of which seem well-equipped to stay up. Despite being one of the Championship's worst defensive teams last season, Hull City rode their luck to Wembley Stadium and managed to win the promotion playoff but seem poised for a rude awakening in the Premier League. Ipswich Town have made some signings they hope will turn good and like many other colleagues, have a new manager in Gary O'Neill who has a track record of leading teams to punch above their own weight, but a lot will have to go right for them to survive. The team perhaps best positioned to stay up is Coventry City, though they will miss goalscorer Haji Wright for the start of the season – the U.S. international will miss up to 12 weeks with what manager Frank Lampard described as a "very serious quad injury."Americans in EnglandA World Cup on home soil now in the rearview mirror, a batch of U.S. men's national team players return to play with their clubs as the long road to the 2030 tournament officially gets underway. Wright will miss the beginning of the season but a handful of World Cup participants should be ready to go as soon as the opening whistle – starters like Crystal Palace's Chris Richards and Bournemouth's Tyler Adams are expected to play big roles this season again for their clubs, and the same goes for Fulham's Antonee Robinson and Leeds United's Brenden Aaronson. There's a new player to keep an eye on, too – 19-year-old winger Zavier Gozo joins Richards at Palace after beginning his career in MLS with Real Salt Lake, becoming the first of a new and exciting generation of U.S. players to take the next step up in his career.

title: The Nuggets are daring Nikola Jokić to leave after a listless summer - CBS Sports
description: Chances are Jokić -- a free agent next summer -- isn't going anywhere, but Denver isn't doing much to ensure that
body:
Chances are Jokić -- a free agent next summer -- isn't going anywhere, but Denver isn't doing much to ensure that
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    2:18 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            9 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The NBA's second apron claimed its latest casualty on Wednesday when the Denver Nuggets shipped Peyton Watson to the Cleveland Cavaliers in an $88 million sign-and-trade that yielded the Nuggets nothing in the way of actual players. They got Cleveland's 2031 first-round pick and Sacramento's 2032 second-round pick, but no Watson replacement. They could potentially pivot to DeMar DeRozan. In 2026, Watson to DeRozan is a downgrade. If you believe otherwise, as the kids say, you don't know ball. The Nuggets will have to shed even more money if they're going to sign DeRozan and still get under the second apron, which is clearly their priority. They're not alone in this endeavor. The Knicks won last year's championship and immediately let Mitchell Robinson walk after owner James Dolan deemed any trip into the second apron as "suicidal." 
        
            
                Peyton Watson trade grades: Cavaliers grab breakout wing, Nuggets have serious questions around Nikola Jokić
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Robinson went to the Celtics, who have moved off of Jaylen Brown, Jrue Holiday, Kristaps Porziņģis, Al Horford and Luke Kornet since winning the 2024 title. Oklahoma City won the 2025 championship and just lost Aaron Wiggins, Lu Dort and Isaiah Joe this summer. The Warriors are currently driving their fans insane by playing it so tight to the vest since their 2022 title. The Bucks won in 2021 and have since blown up. All of this is to say, if the second apron has arguably made it easier than ever to put together a contending roster as talent has been spread more equitably across the league (I would argue no fewer than 13 teams will enter this coming season with conference-finals-caliber rosters). It has also made it harder than ever to keep these rosters together for the same reason.
Through this lens, the Nuggets having lost Bruce Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Michael Porter Jr. and, now, Watson from that 2023 title team is no great sin. It pretty much happens to every team, barring some sort of one-off salary advantage like Jalen Brunson giving the Knicks a discount, or Stephen Curry signing a clearance-rack contract in 2012, or the Spurs having Victor Wembanyama (who has since also given San Antonio a long-term discount), Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper all on rookie contracts at the same time. The key, then, lies in the margin replacements. It's an extremely tight needle to thread, but fans look at a team like OKC -- which has nailed everything from adding Alex Caruso and Isaiah Hartenstein to drafting Cason Wallace and developing Ajay Mitchell, which has in turn afforded them the talent cushion to lose a starter in Dort and a two-way wing in Wiggins that every other team in the league would kill for without skipping a beat -- and expect their front offices to follow suit. This is where the Nuggets have fallen short. Again, they never found another 2023 Brown. They didn't want to pay Caldwell-Pope. They tried to swap Porter Jr. for Cam Johnson, thinking they fit the same player archetype, but it turned out Porter Jr. was just way better. Now they lose Watson, their one young, athletic player with the upside to represent at least a plausible path to improvement from last year's first-round-losing team, because they paid Christian Braun $125 million (at least double what he's worth) and couldn't stomach another money dump. 
Problem is, Watson "only" got $22 million annually, which isn't star money. That's regular starter money. Which Watson is, or should be, and being that the Nuggets were already over the second apron and thus crippled by the roster-building restrictions that apply anyway, why not just pay Watson? First of all, that's easy to say when it's not your money. Sure, the Kroenke family is reportedly worth almost $40 billion, but would running your 2026-27 payroll past $400 million -- which would be an NBA record and is what Denver would've been facing had it re-signed Watson at the $88 million he got from the Cavs -- have been a responsible decision for a team that would probably still fall short of true contender status? Probably not. Should they have done it anyway? The answer to that question would be a resounding no if the Nuggets didn't have Nikola Jokić still at the peak of his powers. But they do. And that's where this gets dicey. 
The franchise icon dilemmaWhen you have not just a superstar, but even one step up from that, a true franchise icon, it becomes impossible for fans to accept anything that could be even remotely perceived as organizational passivity, let alone an owner cheaping out. I'm not sure Denver has been passive, necessarily; I would, in fact, largely commend the Nuggets for their commitment to core continuity since the Aaron Gordon trade, which has indisputably served them well. It's also hard to say the owner of a repeater-tax team heading into next season with a nearly $300 million payroll has cheaped out. But yes, the Nuggets have cut some costly corners since the 2023 championship, and they're continuing to do so. No, fans are not going to accept that when their homegrown Hall of Famer is still arguably the greatest player in the world and currently set to become a free agent next summer. That's where having a player of this caliber can, in a weird way, go from a blessing to a curse as every season you're expected to set sail toward a championship even if the boat is starting to sink. It can become a suicide mission if you're not careful. Go ask the Bucks, who mortgaged everything but their soul to try to keep Giannis Antetokounmpo on a team whose window of contention had clearly closed. They waived and stretched Damian Lillard over five years, paying him $113 million to go play for the Blazers, all so they could turn around and pay Myles Turner north of $100 million. They had to trade Giannis anyway, and they'll be digging out from beneath that debt for years. 
That should've been an easy decision. The Bucks were done. The Nuggets are not, or don't have to be, but their margins have become impossibly thin as two younger, better teams in the Spurs and Thunder have risen to West prominence. Watson was a margin call. The guy has only started 64 games in his career. He had one big stretch last season during which his potential materialized, and his two-way upside is obvious, but it's also not unreasonable to not think he's worth an $88 million bet when you're already buried beneath the Braun contract as the only second-apron team in the league and probably not a contender anyway. Frankly, none of the margin calls the Nuggets have made over these last four summers have been unreasonable on their own. Brown was a big loss but the Nuggets couldn't have kept him if they wanted to in 2023 because they didn't have his early Bird rights and were limited in the raise they could offer him. When Indiana threw $45 million over two years at him, short of Brown taking about a $15 million haircut in the first year of his new deal, Denver, through no fault of its own, was out. The $66 million Orlando gave Caldwell-Pope proved pretty quickly to be a ridiculous contract. The Porter/Johnson swap looks bad in hindsight, but, at the time, pretty much everyone was in agreement that Porter was an overpaid third scorer and Johnson, who had just averaged 19 PPG on 39% 3-point shooting in Brooklyn, fit the bill of a similar player for almost half the price. The frustration, to whatever extent it exists, is in the aggregate of all these compromises. In addition to Watson, the Nuggets have also lost Jonas Valanciunas, who was at least somewhat of a plug for the non-Jokić minutes that have crippled Denver for years, and Sixth Man of the Year finalist Tim Hardaway Jr. from last year's team. 
Forgive the fans if the fans if they fail to see the excitement in adding Tyus Jones and Marvin Bagley Jr., and if they're starting, however quietly, to worriedly ponder a question that has always felt like a forgone conclusion. Will Jokić finish his career in Denver?All signs still point to yes. Two months ago, Jokić told Serbian reporters that his "desire is to play the rest of my life in Denver," and that he would "probably [re]sign [with the Nuggets] next year." That probably provides some pause, but Jokić opting not to sign the $278 million contract extension for which he was eligible this summer is very likely a purely financial decision. Next summer he can sign for $359 million. Chances are he will. He hasn't given any indication to the contrary. The concern would be if the Nuggets are taking this fact that Jokic has never threatened to leave for granted, using it as a license to downshift their roster aggression without fear of consequence. This is what has Golden State fans up in arms. No LeBron James team would hoard draft picks and focus on the "next era" because he would be threatening them behind closed doors within an inch of their organizational life. Stephen Curry doesn't do that. He stays in his lane and professes nothing but love and support for all the decisions his ownership and front office make, even if they come at the cost of his last shot at contention. 
Jokic has always appeared to be cut from the same go-along-get-along cloth. But to mistake that for a lack of competitive desire would be, well, a mistake. The idea that Jokic doesn't care about winning, or really even the sport of basketball in comparison to his horses, is rooted in romance rather than reality. It's fun to think about a Hall of Fame player not giving a damn, but it's not true. He wants to win. He wants to do it in Denver. But that's starting to look more and more unlikely as this core ages. You can only play the "if Aaron Gordon could just stay healthy" card for so long. What's funny is Curry's Warriors would be one of the teams that could theoretically pay Jokić next summer if they worked their cap sheet right. No doubt Joe Lacob is dreaming on that as we speak. It's about as likely to happen as the Warriors getting Giannis was. More likely is Jokić stays in Denver as they either fade more and more from contention or pull a rabbit out of the hat to get back into it -- perhaps by trading Jamal Murray or Gordon at the deadline, or even better, by attaching that 2031 Cleveland pick they got in the Watson deal to Braun and/or Johnson's expiring deal for a meaningful upgrade. 
Let's see how it goes. And again, chances are Jokić isn't going anywhere either way. But iI will say this: If ever there was a blueprint for forcing your franchise icon to consider relocation, it would look a lot like a summer in which you allow three significant players to go and replace them with Marvin freaking Bagley. It doesn't mean Jokić is going to leave. I can't state that enough. But until further notice, it sort of feels like the Nuggets are daring him to do so.

schema.headline: The Nuggets are daring Nikola Jokić to leave after a listless summer - CBS Sports

title: NCAA granted stay in Colorado lawsuit, denying 5th-year eligibility for 2022 class - CBS Sports
description: This ruling will only trigger more legal battles in the co
body:
This ruling will only trigger more legal battles in the coming weeks
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:56 am ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
            
        
                
                
                
            
        
            
                    
                Imagn Images
            
            

    
        The Tenth Circuit has granted the NCAA's stay request in the Wisne vs. NCAA lawsuit. That means qualifying players from the Class of 2022 are once again ineligible unless they have already been granted temporary restraining orders or injunctions.Earlier this summer, Colorado District Judge Charlotte Sweeney ruled that some members of the 2022 class could be granted a fifth year of eligibility. Despite a later clarification that athletes who signed NFL contracts would be ineligible for a return to college football, rookies across the league have been exploring NCAA comebacks.On Wednesday, former LSU standout and current Tampa Bay Buccaneer Jack Pyburn and 15 other athletes were granted a temporary restraining order by a Louisiana judge. Because Pyburn and the other 15 players have their own temporary restraining order, the Tenth Circuit's ruling doesn't affect them, and they are eligible for a return to college football.
While this new ruling in Wisne vs. NCAA may be a victory for the NCAA, it will trigger another wave of lawsuits as other members of the 2022 class seek their own temporary restraining orders and injuctions.
This is about to get particularly interesting as the NFL regular season approaches. With roster cut-down day set for Aug. 30, more rookies on the fringes could turn their attention back to the college ranks instead of fighting for roster spots at the pro level. If that happens, they may take legal action in hopes of getting one more year of eligibility.We've already seen a slew of athletes score victories in that department. Recently, Arizona State defensive back and All-Big 12 honoree Myles Rowser was granted a temporary restraining order that not only granted him a fifth year of eligibility but also allowed him to enter the transfer portal.
Other players -- like Indiana edge rushers Stephen Daley and Kellar Wyatt -- have announced their return on the strength of the Colorado eligibility ruling. They are now ineligible for the moment, but they are among countless other players who could take legal action to get a temporary restraining order or injunction of their own.

title: College football odds: Penn State, BYU among best win total bets ahead of 2026 - CBS Sports
description: Riding a 15-3 stretch on preseason win total bets, our CBS Sports gambling expert locks down the best bets to pur
body:
Riding a 15-3 stretch on preseason win total bets, our CBS Sports gambling expert locks down the best bets to pursue ahead of the 2026 season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:15 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Gauging what to make of programs with new coaches is particularly challenging in the modern age of college football, when rosters can be flipped in a span of weeks with a quick wave of the portal wand. We've seen previously unfathomable one-year turnarounds at schools like Indiana, followed by monumental first-year flops at schools like North Carolina.If you're willing to look under the hood and dissect the nuances of each situation, there is value to be found from a betting perspective with new regimes. A year ago, Wake Forest's over on a 4.5 win total was priced at +116, and it hit before the end of October as the Demon Deacons rode a favorable schedule to an 8-4 mark under first-year coach Jake Dickert.That was among the five bets included in this column, which is now in its fifth year. Four of them hit, as my four-year record on win totals improved to 15-3 with five pushes. This year, we are returning to the first-year coach vein for three of our five selections.
        
            
                College football win totals: Eight teams poised for big rise or fall in number of victories in 2026
                
                    Chris Hummer                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The first season is not always an indicator of a coach's future viability for a variety of reasons. Wildly imbalanced conference schedules are a major swing factor, and that's a large part of the rationale for my faith in Penn State. New coach Matt Campbell's learning curve will be made simpler by the absence of three Big Ten heavyweights from the Nittany Lions' 2026 schedule.
My degree of confidence in these is high, and a 3-2 record with these odds is guaranteed to break even. If you want to go bold and take Arkansas to go under 3.5 and/or go with Minnesota over 6.5, the payout could be even better. Here are the 2026 season's best bets, with odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Penn State: Over 9.5 wins (+140)A schedule that misses Indiana, Ohio State and Oregon will ease Matt Campbell's transition from Iowa State to Penn State. The Nittany Lions' nonconference slate of Marshall, Temple and Buffalo is also light, and five of Penn State's nine league games are at home. Campbell's Iowa State-heavy transfer class is the No. 4-ranked haul in the country, and a nice sampling of talent from the James Franklin era is still around. Among them are a star left tackle in Anthony Donkoh, a veteran leader at linebacker in Tony Rojas and a proven starter at corner in Audavion Collins. All told, the conditions are optimized for the Nittany Lions to win 10 or 11 regular-season games and crack the CFP in Year 1 of the new regime. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Minnesota: Over 5.5 wins (-160)Minnesota's rushing offense is mired in an uncharacteristic lull that should end in 2026 behind an offensive line that features an NFL Draft prospect at guard in Greg Johnson and a 2025 freshman All-American at tackle in Nathan Roy. Furthermore, Drake Lindsey is back at quarterback after a promising redshirt freshman campaign. He should only improve when defenses have to respect the Gophers' rushing attack again. Minnesota also misses Ohio State and Oregon, leaving an Oct. 31 game at Indiana as the only contest that looks outright unwinnable. Even when you write in losses against Michigan, at Indiana and at Penn State, the Gophers still have plenty of wiggle room to reach six wins. If you're a big believer, taking the over 6.5 will bring a significantly better payout.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Arkansas under 4.5 (-200)First-year coach Ryan Silverfield is due for a rude welcome to the SEC. Not only is he arriving just as the league goes to a nine-game conference schedule, but the Razorbacks also face a Week 2 road trip to play Utah. As the school's administration has pointed out with great ire, that late-night contest (at altitude) will be followed by a noon Eastern kick against Georgia the following week. The hits keep coming with trips to Texas A&M and Texas, along with tricky home games against established programs like Tennessee and Missouri. A second straight 2-10 campaign is possible. But even if the Razorbacks pull a couple of league upsets, it's hard to fathom a universe in which they reach 5-7 with a totally overhauled roster featuring inexperienced quarterback options. The under 3.5 comes with a significantly better payout and should also be considered by those with bullish tastes.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Iowa State: under 5.5 (-220)After Matt Campbell's 3-9 debut in 2016, the Cyclones only failed to reach six regular-season victories once in his next nine years, creating an impression that perhaps Iowa State had leveled up its floor. But as the program reboots under Jimmy Rogers, a bottoming out could be in store. This is a total scrape-and-rebuild. While Rogers is bringing 15 players with him from Washington State, he was only there for a single 7-6 season. It's not as if the bedrock of an established program is arriving, as we often see with other first-year coaches. While the Big 12 schedule isn't brutal -- the Cyclones miss Texas Tech and Houston -- Iowa State will likely need to win four conference games to cash the over. It's hard to see this ISU roster grinding out four league wins in Year 1 with the nation's 67th-ranked transfer class. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    BYU over 8.5 (-150)Of the other three Big 12 teams that reached double-digit victories last season, BYU only has to play one as part of a schedule featuring five Big 12 home games. There is no Texas Tech on the slate and no Houston. The toughest road game is a quick bus ride down I-15 to play rival Utah, which is in the midst of a coaching transition. With key playmakers back throughout the defense, the only real question is who will emerge to catch passes from star sophomore quarterback Bear Bachmeier. He's got 1,300-yard rusher LJ Martin back, and the Cougars are poised to field another group of maulers on the offensive line. This program is absolutely humming under Kalani Sitake and should reach double-digit victories for a third straight season. If you're a big believer, find over 9.5 for a better return.

title: Raiders QB competition: Kirk Cousins has clear edge over Fernando Mendoza - CBS Sports
description: Klint Kubiak says the competition will continue, but Cousins has done little to lose his grip on the starting job
body:
Klint Kubiak says the competition will continue, but Cousins has done little to lose his grip on the starting job
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:02 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        With the start of the regular season just over three weeks away, the Las Vegas Raiders still haven't named a starting quarterback. Raiders coach Klint Kubiak had the chance to name a starter following the team's 22-20 preseason win over the Texans on Thursday night, but instead, he decided to keep everyone guessing. "We got another week of playing. I don't want anyone to be comfortable in their job," Kubiak said. "It should always be that way for all positions. So, let's keep going forward."That makes it sound like the battle between Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza will be raging on for another week, but based on what Kubiak has said throughout training camp, it seems like his decision has already been made; he's just not ready to share it. 
Who the Raiders starting QB will likely be in Week 1Right now, all signs point to Cousins. Over the course of training camp, the closest Kubiak has come to naming a starter came after the Raiders' first preseason game back on Aug. 13. In a 27-14 loss to the Cardinals, Cousins was on the field for exactly one offensive possession, and he was nearly perfect: The veteran quarterback went 5-of-6 for 50 yards and a touchdown. "Kirk's been getting the reps with the ones. I think he's had a solid training camp and it's his job to lose," Kubiak said.Those last five words are the key ones: It's his job to lose. In the week since those comments were made, Cousins hasn't really done anything to lose the job. 
The four-time Pro Bowler didn't play on Thursday night against the Texans, but he took part in a joint practice against Houston earlier this week. Cousins put together an up-and-down day against the Texans. On the negative side, he threw a pick-six to Kamari Lassiter, according to The Athletic, but he also made several big plays against a Texans team that will almost certainly have one of the best defenses in the NFL this year. "Probably would have liked to have finished a little stronger," Cousins said after Tuesday's practice, via The Athletic. "But we made some plays in the first few periods that we were pleased with, and we'll keep building from here."With Cousins struggling some, this could have been a spot where Mendoza closed the gap with the 38-year-old veteran, but instead, the No. 1 overall pick also struggled against Houston's defense. During the joint practice, Mendoza actually got some reps with the first team, which has been a rarity for him in training camp, but he wasn't able to outplay Cousins. Mendoza did make some highlight throws, but he also threw two interceptions during a red zone period, including a pick-six to Jalen Pitre, according to The Athletic. 
Although Cousins wasn't on the field for Thursday's preseason game, Mendoza was and the rookie got off to a rough start with a pick-six on his third pass of the game. 
Mendoza ended up finishing 8-of-15 for 86 yards, but the only touchdown he threw went to the other team. After the game, Kubiak said the rookie still has a lot to work on. "Plenty to clean up. Plenty to get better at," Kubiak said when asked about Mendoza's performance. "Plenty that we can do better for him as coaches. Plenty that he can learn from."
With Mendoza facing a steep learning curve, it doesn't seem like he's done enough to take the job from Cousins. Kubiak said it was Cousins' job to lose, and if that's the case, it doesn't seem like he's done enough to lose it. Cousins likely won't play in the Raiders' final preseason game, which means he'll have been on the field for only one series over three games. Most coaches keep their veteran QB on the bench like that to keep their guy healthy for the season, which is another sign the Raiders will probably roll with Cousins in their opener against the Dolphins. Since the start of training camp, there's only been one instance in which Kubiak referred to Cousins as the starter, and that came on Day 1, July 28. 
"When we go out to practice tomorrow, Kirk Cousins is the starting quarterback," Kubiak said. "He's the guy, and he's going to get a ton of reps. He deserves them because he's played really good football. But I want Fernando and I want Aidan (O'Connell) to push him."The depth chart hasn't changed much at quarterback since that day, which is why "Kirk Cousins is the starting quarterback" is something we'll probably hear Kubiak say again in the very near future.

Jacob Gibbs thinks we may have unlocked a cheat code to drafting your 2026 Fantasy Football rosters

        The first two rounds of your 2026 Fantasy Football drafts could produce multiple league-winning draft picks at the running back position and it appears this is more defined than we've seen in past years. This range of Fantasy Football drafts produces league-winners at a really high (relatively speaking) rate. And in 2026, this range of drafts is dominated by the RB position. What is one to do when on the clock and staring at a list of awesome running backs?! Let's sort through the early-round RB league-winning candidates.I'm going to profile each back for Fantasy purposes -- offering my perception of their ceiling, floor, and stability. Hopefully this helps you in some way. It's arbitrary; I made it up. I've ruminated on potential outcomes for these players a lot, though, so hopefully this is an effective way for my thoughts to resonate.Here's how I understand this concept:Ceiling rating - if the player hits a 75th percentile (or better) outcome, how impactful is it on a scale of 1-100?Floor rating - how concerned am I by the possibility of the player hitting a 25th percentile (or worse) outcome?Stability rating - on a scale of 1-100, how impactful is variability in this player's outlook?High number = goodHigh ceiling rating = Lots of upsideHigh floor rating = Lots of warm fuzzy feelings of (probably false) security when I click this player's name
High stability rating = the outcome feels more predictable. The path to a "good" outcome feels wide and easy to navigate. Please do not toy with us today, chaos.Another way to think about this stability rating: how many factors outside of the individual's control are they relying on to shape their outcome? Furthermore, how reliable do those factors feel? A player with many unreliable factors available to influence their outcome will have a low stability rating.If we simulated the NFL season 100 times, the 25 best outcomes would represent 75th-100th percentile outcomes. Those outcomes represent the player's "ceiling." The 25 worst outcomes would represent the 1st-25th percentile outcomes. Those outcomes represent the player's "floor."
What might these outcomes look like? How might a player arrive at such an outcome? We obviously don't have those answers, but we can speculate on them and aim to place our best bets.James Cook (my RB4)Ceiling rating - 89 (out of 100)Floor rating - 75 (I'm a little concerned about the workload)Stability rating - 85James Cook gets to his ceiling outcome through an expanded receiving role and continued dominance on the ground. Cook hits his floor outcome as a result of diminished offensive line play, or wear and tear catching up to him after a massive 2025 workload.
Chase Brown (my RB5)Ceiling rating - 87Floor rating - 90Stability rating - 80Chase Brown gets to his ceiling outcome through an eruption season from the Cincinnati Bengals offense. Brown hits his floor outcome as a result of skill issue (pass protection has at times led to him losing reps when backfield teammates were healthy) or Cincy's offense not playing up to expectation.Ashton Jeanty (my RB6)Ceiling rating - 86Floor rating - 80Stability rating - 82 (I know it feels high. He's a young player with massive organizational investment who has already shown an ability to handle a gargantuan workload)Ashton Jeanty gets to his ceiling outcome through improved offensive line play and usage maximization within Klint Kubiak's plan. Jeanty hits his floor outcome as a result of skill issue (he had such a low explosive play rate last year - easily reasoned away with offensive environment excuses, but still - we need to see improvement here for him to deliver Fantasy efficiency) or offensive ecosystem dysfunction.
Jonathan Taylor (my RB7)Ceiling rating - 91Floor rating - 69Stability rating - 60Jonathan Taylor gets to his ceiling outcome through positive game scripts allowing the Colts to lean on the ground game in a return to form for the offense. He also offers unique "any given play" ability that can make him a weekly Fantasy winner. JT hits his floor outcome as a result of Indy's offense underperforming, the defense struggling to the point that the Colts have to take to the air more than preferred, or wear and tear simply catching up to him.Oct 21, 2024; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Los Angeles Chargers offensive tackle Rashawn Slater (70) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images 
                                                                    Mark J. Rebilas
                                                            Omarion Hampton (my RB8)Ceiling rating - 90 (JT gets the edge because of true bell-cow dominance. Hampton's ceiling outcome feels similar to Cook's)Floor rating - 60Stability rating - 66Omarion Hampton gets to his ceiling outcome through an massive touchdown production within a high-powered Chargers offense. He also offers efficiency upside through explosive play potential. Hampton hits his floor outcome as a result of skill issue (he's the most unproven RB being selected in this range), backfield competition, or L.A.'s offense not living up to hype.
De'Von Achane (my RB9)Ceiling rating - 89Floor rating - 72Stability rating - 30De'Von Achane gets to his ceiling outcome through explosive plays, a surprising positive performance from Miami's offense, or a uniquely large receiving role within an offense lacking proven receiving options. Achane hits his floor outcome as a result of wear and tear, poor coaching, or lack of space for his skills to shine with defenses focusing all attention on him.Kenneth Walker (my RB10)Ceiling rating - 88Floor rating - 63Stability rating - 55Kenneth Walker gets to his ceiling outcome through an expanded receiving role and improved rushing efficiency behind a better offensive line. Walker hits his floor outcome as a result of splitting backfield reps, lack of receiving role, Kansas City's offense underperforming, or wear and tear becoming a problem once again.
                                                                    Imagn Images
                                                            Derrick Henry (my RB11)Ceiling rating - 87Floor rating - 79Stability rating - 77Derrick Henry gets to his ceiling outcome through an offensive eruption in Baltimore. He also could see an expanded receiving role. And, of course, explosive play ability always offers Henry upside to produce top-end efficiency. Henry hits his floor outcome as a result of diminished offensive line play, overhyped coaching, or wear and tear catching up to him.
Saquon Barkley (my RB12)Ceiling rating - 87Floor rating - 72Stability rating - 70Saquon Barkley gets to his ceiling outcome through a return to health for his offensive line, an injection of energy from a new play-caller, or better luck converting red zone touchdowns. He also might offer explosive play upside once again. Barkley hits his floor outcome as a result of offensive line injuries, overhyped coaching, or wear and tear catching up to him.If you wanna hear me talk through my thoughts on each of these backs in more detail, here's an hour on Beyond the Box Score! I think I'm going to move Derrick Henry ahead of Kenneth Walker after this practice.

I have exciting news! My rankings will be on CBS! I'll let you know when they are. Another exciting piece of news for the FFT NL crew -- I have finalized in-season planning for Beyond the Box Score, and my intention is to bring you a massive SEVEN weekly Beyond The Boxscore shows. I can confirm that Dan the man and I will be recording multiple times per week! I also intend to produce weekly solo shows where I provide an in-depth usage breakdown for every position to keep you in the know regarding all of your sicko needs.I also can confirm that Ryan Heath will be joining BTB on a weekly basis once again! We're tackling a new project together this year, so be on the lookout for that! And more good news, I'm teaming up with Theo Gremminger twice each week to provide y'all with top notch content! The OG will join BTB early in the week to reflect on the previous week's outcomes, and I'll join Rotowire late in the week to speculate on the upcoming week's outcomes.The original BTB crew (Adam Aizer, Dan, and I) will bring you advanced data on Mondays, as per usual -- be sure to be on the lookout for Aizer's tweets leading up to that show, if you send in good questions, we will talk about them on Monday!BTB will be live on Tuesdays and Thursdays, in addition to the Monday morning live show with Adam on the main FFT channel! You will also find me live on Sunday mornings as a reoccurring guest for the FFT start/sit show!
It's a busy time of year, but it's also my favorite time of year! Football is here! Dan Schneier and I will present our FINAL rankings for each position next week on BTB! Let's lock in and win some leagues!
                                                                    Imagn Images                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                            What defines a league-winner?Nobody knows what it means. It's provocative. It gets the people going!If you want an attempt at quantifying it, maybe you'll enjoy this conversation with Ryan Heath of Fantasy Points Data.Jonathon Brooks, RB, Carolina PanthersI could be overstating his importance (Carolina's offensive line injuries concern me), but Jonathon Brooks feels like the cheapest potential bell-cow RB who might actually be an awesome talent available in 2026 drafts. Bell-cow running backs are extremely important for Fantasy! If we can land on outside of the first few rounds, it's a massive influx of upside for our Fantasy squads.
Depending on how Chuba Hubbard's hamstring cooperates, there's a chance that Brooks sees a large workload early and never lets go of it. Brooks was the first player I discussed in the 'Welcome Back' show on Beyond the Box Score, because I believe he might be a defining aspect of the 2026 draft season. I don't see any other potential three-down skill-sets available anywhere near Brooks, even as his ADP rises. There are a few names who could profile similarly -- Jaylen Warren, Rhamondre Stevenson, and Rashaad White -- but it would require a backfield teammate to falter or miss time with an injury. Brooks is sharing a backfield with an already-injured player who we saw underperform while struggling with health last year -- Hubbard already has seen this coaching staff give his lead back duties to another RB.Round 1-2 turn could produce multiple RB league-winnersThis range of Fantasy Football drafts produces league winners at a really high rate (relatively speaking). And in 2026, this range of drafts is dominated by the RB position. What is one to do when on the clock and staring at a list of awesome running backs?! Earlier this week on CBSSports.com, I profiled each back for Fantasy purposes -- offering my perception of their ceiling, floor, and stability. Here's my breakdown of the league-winning Rounds 1-2 running backs.A.J. Brown, WR, New England Patriots
                                                                    Getty Images
                                                            Here's my AJB case. I view him as one of the most-likely candidates to finish WR1 overall.
The podcast that I linked in reference to AJB is great, there are tons of nuggets in there. This link should take you to a discussion about the Chicago Bears.I do not think that there are too many mouths to feed in Chicago. Even if Caleb Williams does not take a step forward (by the way, I feel cautiously optimistic that a step forward is coming -- Ben Johnson's tone has completely shifted over the past 365 days), the WR production we saw from Chicago last year was strong enough to facilitate a strong performance from at least the team's WR1.Luther Burden, WR, Chicago BearsIf he beats out Rome Odunze for targets (here's why I think that he will), Luther Burden can absolutely produce with even just the same offensive environment provided by the first year of Johnson's tenure in Chicago. I expect more from this offense in Year 2 under Johnson. And I expect Burden to play a huge role within the offense.
Tucker Kraft, TE, Green Bay PackersThe Packers have so much target vacancy to be accounted for. Christian Watson's career-high targets in a game is 10, and he's only been above eight twice. Jayden Reed's career-high targets in a game is also 10, and that's the only time he's had more than eight targets in a game. Those two have been extremely efficient per-target players, but neither has been targeted at a high rate.Matthew Golden had just a 15.7% target share at the University of Texas in 2024. His target share was above 20% in only 3 of 16 games.Is Tucker Kraft (target totals of 9 and 10 in two games before his ACL injury last year) going to suddenly play a larger-than-seen-before role? That seemed to be the way things were trending in 2025. It's worth remembering that Jayden Reed was out in both of those games and Christian Watson missed the first and played a partial role in his return from ACL surgery in the second "big Kraft target game."
Jordan Love and Matt LaFleur talk about Kraft like he's "Jordan's guy."Kraft was definitely the player trusted when in scoring distance. I wonder how realistic it is to expect the target shares we were seeing before his injury sustain over a larger sample size. If we get anything similar to that, Kraft -- a player who has been unbelievably efficient on a per-target basis -- could burn Fantasy leagues to the ground if healthy. The best outcome for Kraft is that he's a rare every-down tight end who can push his route rate into the 90% range, create yards after the catch (at a league-best rate), and convert red zone targets into scores.What if he's not ready for all that, yet, though?It would mark a pretty significant leap in his progression for Kraft -- even if not recovering from a reconstructed knee 00 to suddenly operate like a primary target, though. This is why I'm so high on Reed and Watson as 2026 discounts. History tells us that Watson and Reed are more likely to step into that type of a role. Most pass games use outside receivers as the primary read, so Watson in particular looks promising.Last year, Green Bay had seven instances of a pass-catcher reaching a first-read target share of 33% or higher -- Kraft did it once, Dontayvion Wicks did it once, Romeo Doubs did it twice, and Watson hit that rate three times (consecutive rates of 33%, 40%, and 35% across Weeks 11-13).
Watson returned in Week 8 but was not a full-time player until Week 10. From Week 11 on, he had a first-read target rate of 29.4%, and his rate never dipped below 20%. I wondered if his massively-high average depth of target came down during that stretch, but it was still 15.8 yards. That's so high!It's very rare to be productive for Fantasy with such a high aDOT. Even the best players who fall in that range (Alec Pierce and Jameson Williams last year) aren't able to push target shares much higher than 23-25%. This again leads me to Reed as a potential league-winner in 2026. Maybe it's Golden. The case feels so clear with Reed, though.Kraft has the talent to win people leagues. If he's not ready to fill that type of a role, then that means even more volume could shift over to the receivers. And the receivers already are expected to pick up the slack in replacing Wicks and Doubs. I know that betting on Packers receivers has been frustrating in the past, but it really feels like this is a clear source of potential league-winning value depending on how the target distribution shakes out.
Oronde Gadsden II, TE, Los Angeles Chargers I thought long and hard about who I wanted to write about among the Chargers pass-catchers. My belief is that Ladd McConkey is the most-likely player to put together a huge season. His price tag suggests as much. I still think there's plenty of room for McConkey to be a great pick at ADP, but Quentin Johnston and Year 2 tight end Oronde Gadsden II were the two who I kept feeling compelled to write about.I landed on Gadsden for reasons similar to Kraft. If he hits, Gadsden profiles as a meaningful red zone weapon who might also add some yardage juice with his unique skill set as a receiver. If Gadsden plays a meaningful role, not only will he be a hit (Year 2 tight ends often do!) as a late-round TE, but it also could detract from the ceiling cases for McConkey and QJ. Conversely, what if Gadsden ends up phased out? David Njoku and Charlie Kolar present more of a 50/50 proposition to opposing defenses. If one or both of those two are in the game, it's not clear if the Chargers will run or pass. If Gadsden is in, it's likely a pass. The Chargers also have a fullback who Mike McDaniel is a known fan of. It's possible that Gadsden simply won't matter much for an offense focused on establishing an effective run game.That's why I settled on him as a player who might 'define' 2026 Fantasy Football. How do you feel about Gadsden? If you don't expect him to be prioritized, then you probably should be drafting a lot of McConkey or QJ or both. (Also, shoutout BTB favorite Tre Harris, always)
Jaxson Dart, QB, New York GiantsJaxson Dart is one of five QBs to average 20+ Fantasy points per game (only including starts) as a rookie, dating back to 2000. He was one of, if not outright the best, playmaker at the QB position last year.Still, Dart is relatively cheap in 2026 drafts. We do not know what to expect from this coaching staff, but I have not heard a single analyst all summer with even a little bit of cope that the coaching might not be that bad. Universally the Fantasy community feels terrified of this situation.It feels like so much will fall on Dart's shoulders to simply be good enough to make things work in this offense. And, he kind of did last year, without Malik Nabers! If Dart is simply really good, this offense could produce some massive Fantasy producers. The schedule looks really favorable in the second-half of the season. Players like Nabers and Cam Skattebo could produce huge results at decent discounts in drafts. Do you feel like betting on this situation?
The Minnesota VikingsI can't get over how favorable Minnesota's schedule is. Ever since digging into it with Dan, Minnesota's schedule has remained ingrained in my brain as a potentially important part of 2026 Fantasy Football. This offense was so incredibly disappointing in 2025. It's tough for drafters to wash such a nasty taste from their mouths. If the offense rebounds in 2026, this schedule could facilitate incredible Fantasy outcomes for some severely discounted players.The toughest defenses I see -- on paper -- on Minnesota's schedule are the Packers and 49ers. And one of those matchups vs. Green Bay comes in Week 1 without Micah Parsons. Beyond that, the toughest matchups might be Saints, Panthers, and Bills. It's an incredible soft schedule, and on top of the advantageous defensive matchups, the Vikings also could benefit from facing some good offenses. We could see some shootouts if the Vikings offense can put points on the board.I'm coming around on this backfield as a potentially really value source in 2026. A return to health for the tackles could provide a big boost, and I'm intrigued to see what Frank Smith (formerly worked with Mike McDaniel in Miami) might do in revamping Minnesota's scheme. Demond Claiborne is one of my favorite late-round stashes, and I see either Jordan Mason or Aaron Jones as viable picks in drafts where they fall. You might get early-season production, and with good luck, potentially a full season of value.The passing game is the crux of the Minnesota outcome. And, of course, we have no idea what to expect. I see some concerning signs for Justin Jefferson, in terms of the pairing with Kyler Murray. He's the one who I have the hardest time ever clicking in drafts. Everyone else in this offense feels like a value. But if we see Minnesota put points on the board, Jefferson will probably be a huge part of it. His target shares have never been higher than the last two seasons. We just need the overall passing production in Minnesota to be better for it to matter.The Tampa Bay BuccaneersNobody knows what to expect from Bucky Irving. Nobody really even knows what to expect from Emeka Egbuka, especially now that a toe injury is part of the equation. I am really excited about how Zac Robinson can affect change in Tampa. Pair that with a return to health for a potentially mauling offensive line, and this Bucs offense is one that I want to aggressively attack in drafts.If you don't believe in Bucky, you absolutely should be scooping up a ton of Kenneth Gainwell at his ADP. I believe in Bucky. The most interesting value on this offense might actually be Chris Godwin. Camp reports are good -- Godwin is expected to play an important role once again, and as my buddy Ryan Heath astutely pointed out, Godwin has been extremely efficient when used in motion at the snap of the football. Robinson has used motion at snap at the highest rate of any play-caller over the past two years.I even think that we could get surprise Fantasy viability from an ancillary piece such as Cade Otton or Jalen McMillan if Baker blows the league up on his "pay me" tour. And what if the Egbuka injury lingers? This team has a plethora of talented receivers. If there's an injury to any of the top guys, we could see Tez Johnson benefit in a huge way from free releases at the line of scrimmage within Robinson's design. Rookie Ted Hurst has some serious juice.There's a ton to like in Tampa's offense, and we truly have no idea how the volume is going to be distributed. I want to lean into that uncertainty and pile up as many Bucs as I can on my Fantasy squads. And, of course, I love landing Baker as a late-round QB.Good luck to anybody drafting this weekend! Keep an eye on your inbox! Rankings updates will be coming your way soon!

title: Ex-Alabama basketball player awarded $9.25 million in a defamation case against the New York Times - CBS Sports
description: Kai Spears, a former walk-on basketball player at Alabama,
body:
Kai Spears, a former walk-on basketball player at Alabama, was awarded $9.25 million in a defamation case against the New York Times this week.
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 21, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:46 am ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
            
        
                
                
                
            
        
            
                    
                Getty Images
            
            

    
        An Alabama jury awarded $9.25 million in damages to former Crimson Tide basketball player Kai Spears on Thursday after an eight-person jury found the New York Times defamed him by incorrectly reporting that he was at the scene of a fatal shooting.The jury ruled in favor of Spears after the Times wrote in 2023 that he was a passenger in a car involved in the death of 23-year-old Jamea Harris, which he denied after the report came out. The Times reported that the person had spoken, "on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters." "I have one thing to say — the report in the New York Times was 100% inaccurate and the writer had complete disregard for the truth," Spears said in a statement in 2023. "I am trying to process and cope with these false statements that somehow have been published and then seen by so many. So thankful to Alabama Athletics for refuting it on my behalf."More than anything, I remain completely heartbroken by the tragic death that occurred that night."
Spears, who began his college basketball career at Alabama as a walk-on, transferred to Marshall in 2024, where he spent the last two seasons. He transferred to Division II West Liberty this offseason.

title: Klay Thompson expected to sign with Heat after buyout from Mavericks, per report - CBS Sports

The veteran wing will provide the Heat with much-needed shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo

        The Dallas Mavericks announced on Friday that they had reached a buyout agreement with Klay Thompson, making the sharp-shooting wing a late addition to the free agent market. Shortly after the announcement, ESPN reported that Thompson is expected to sign with the Miami Heat once he clears waivers, providing some much-needed shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo on the new-look Heat. Thompson, 36, signed with the Mavericks in 2024 and played 141 games in Dallas, averaging 12.9 points on 40.3/38.7/85.1 shooting splits in two seasons. With Dallas pivoting toward a youth movement led by reigning Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg, the Mavericks had little need to keep Thompson on the roster for the 2026-27 season and opted to reach a buyout well before training camp began to give him the opportunity to sign with a contender. "Klay is one of the great players and competitors of his generation, and we are grateful for everything he brought to the Mavericks organization," Mavericks president of basketball operations Masai Ujiri said in a statement. "We have tremendous respect for Klay and all that he has accomplished throughout his career, and we wish him nothing but the best moving forward."
Thompson clearly already had his preferred destination in mind when negotiating a buyout with the Mavs, with word he planned to join the Heat coming mere minutes after the news went public. While Thompson isn't the two-way force he was at his peak, his shooting acumen is something the Heat desperately need on their roster after trading Tyler Herro to Milwaukee and letting Norman Powell walk in free agency to bring in Antetokounmpo.

Miami faced hard cap restrictions in building out its roster around Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, and hoped to accelerate its timeline as a contender by signing LeBron James. Once James opted to join the Philadelphia 76ers, the Heat had to pivot to find veteran reinforcements for the roster and landed a four-time NBA champion in Thompson to bolster their pursuit of a fourth title in Miami. Thompson will join Andrew Wiggins, Nikola Jovic, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Dru Smith as Miami's wing rotation, providing coach Erik Spoelstra with another option for building lineups around their All-Star frontcourt. 
Thompson's shooting efficiency has dipped a bit from his peak since returning from ACL and Achilles injuries, but in the five seasons since getting back on the court, he's still shot 39.3% from three on 8.8 attempts per game. Given how few shooters Miami has on its roster, Thompson figures to find a prominent role in the Heat's rotation as they look to climb back into the upper echelon of the Eastern Conference.

title: Jim Nantz shares memorable broadcasting moment from Pebble Beach over 40-year career - CBS Sports
description: With the PGA Tour calendar winding down, Nantz reflected on the year and a favorite memory
body:
With the PGA Tour calendar winding down, Nantz reflected on the year and a favorite memory

        The end of a season inevitably brings a sense of nostalgia. Like a school year ending -- when ironically most are beginning -- the culmination comes with thoughts of what has been. Superlatives are given out. Memories are shared. Plans for the future go from pencil to pen to gone in a blink of an eye.The PGA Tour is no different. Like any other organization or group, the calendar comes for them with the FedEx Cup Playoffs representing the final salvo for what was an eventful, even surprising, 2026 campaign. Superstars and household names won. Young guns fired on all cylinders. Major championships were claimed by both perennial contenders and outsiders who gained the inside track.Much of the story has unfolded on CBS airwaves just as the remaining two tournaments -- the BMW Championship and the Tour Championship -- of the FedEx Cup Playoffs will. At the helm for it all has been legendary broadcaster Jim Nantz amid a season that marked No. 40 since his first call at the Masters in 1986.Yes, that Masters.Having experienced a lifetime of calls and a lifetime of once in a lifetime moments from those swinging the clubs, Nantz would not divulge if there has been a favorite broadcast of his to be a part of."The next one," Nantz said. "I love them all."
Instead, he did what he did best and told a story. This one about the old Crosby Clambake as it was called back then, now known as the AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am. While the whimsical nature of the event has passed by and those in the pro-am portion of the tournament across the first 36 holes are more C-Suite than C-list, there was a time, and who better to explain how his original answer formed than Nantz himself."One time, I was a part of the CBS crew early in my career at Pebble [Beach]. I never forgot this line," Nantz said. "Phil Harris played this boozy, kind of always looked like a guy that was coming in and out of bars, and that's not cool today, I get that. "But actually, on the air, on our air one time, Jack Lemmon hit a shot at 18 at Pebble Beach, down off the rocks and into the ocean and [Pat] Summerall intone, 'That's Lemmon on the rocks,'. [Ken] Venturi said, 'Sounds like a drink I had last night in the taproom.' "And with that, he turned to Phil, who was now playing the role of Bing [Crosby]. Bing had just recently passed in the last 10 years. He says, 'You know, Phil, I've always wanted to ask you, you're a renowned drinker, what's your favorite drink?'
"And he said on CBS, 'The next one.'"

        Max Holloway only sees empty threats from Conor McGregor. In the aftermath of a disappointing conclusion to their fight at UFC 329, Holloway sees just a loudmouth where a brash, talented young fighter once stood.Holloway and McGregor headlined International Fight Week this year. Nearly 16 million people across the U.S. and Latin America tuned in for the monumental card. Unfortunately, the fight fizzled immediately once the spectacular entrances concluded. McGregor injured himself with the first kick he threw, and the fight was waved off a little more than a minute later. McGregor went on a crisis management tour in the weeks after. He advocated for a no-contest ruling, and claimed his "generational beating" of Holloway was only postponed to next year. Holloway can't help but laugh at McGregor."It's just crazy for the dude to be talking about how it was slippery because of the dry ice," Holloway said on his YouTube channel, referencing the substance for their elaborate entrances. "I don't know what he's talking about because I didn't fall. 
"Him talking about this 'generational beating.' Dude is delusional because, to me, he felt slow in there. He looked old. If there was gonna be a generational beating, it wasn't gonna be on his end."Holloway has three directions in mind for his next fight. "Blessed" would like a welterweight or lightweight title shot. He's also open to completing the McGregor trilogy, something he also advocated during his post-fight interview.
"If it's a title shot, in either weight class, sign ya boy up," he said. "If it's a Conor McGregor fight again, I'll sign the dotted line.   UFC, I'm owed the Conor McGregor belt, the money belt, so you guys gotta send me that."
